The Honorable Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS-0062-P 
P.O. Box 8013 
Baltimore, MD 21244-8013 
 
Re: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule  
(CMS-0062-P) 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
The Cigna Group (Cigna) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid 
Services’ (CMS’s) Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) 
(Proposed Rule). 
 
The Cigna Group is a global health company committed to improving health and vitality. Our Cigna Healthcare 
and Evernorth Health Services divisions offer medical, pharmacy, dental, behavioral health, and related products 
and services, with over 186 million customer and patient relationships in the more than thirty countries and 
jurisdictions in which we operate. In the United States, Cigna Healthcare provides medical coverage to 
approximately sixteen million Americans in the commercial group health plan market, predominantly in the self-
insured segment.  
 
Our health services business, Evernorth Health Services, includes a broad range of coordinated and point solution 
health services and capabilities in pharmacy benefits, home delivery pharmacy, specialty pharmacy, distribution, 
and care delivery and management solutions, which are provided to health plans, employers, government 
organizations, and healthcare providers. Across all segments we serve, The Cigna Group is focused on working to 
deliver healthcare that is affordable, predictable, and simple so people can live healthier, more vibrant lives. 
 
With that context in mind, The Cigna Group offers the following comments on the Proposed Rule with our key 
recommendations summarized below the introduction on pages 2 and 3. We also provide an appendix containing 
comments in response to CMS’s requests for information (RFIs). 
 
* 
* 
* 
 
I. Introduction 
a. Cigna’s Commitment to Supporting the CMS Health Technology Ecosystem and Improving 
Prior Authorization 
Cigna strongly supports the Administration’s focus on promoting innovation, reducing administrative burden, and 
improving the patient experience. Consistent with these goals, Cigna has been pleased to work with the 
Administration on improving the prior authorization (PA) experience for patients and providers through both 
voluntary industry action and active partnership in federal initiatives. We are committed to the goal of ensuring 
patients receive appropriate, high-quality care when they need it. Prior authorization remains an important tool to 
  
 
 
 
2 
 
support appropriate, evidence-based care, and it should operate in ways that allow providers and their teams to 
focus on patients rather than paperwork.  
 
In June 2025, working in concert with the Administration, Cigna led the adoption of PA industry commitments. 
Working through our national trade association, AHIP, these voluntary commitments established a coordinated, 
industry-wide approach to improving PA by reducing administrative burden and improving timeliness, 
transparency, and predictability. These commitments include actions such as reducing the volume of services 
subject to PA, honoring PA approvals during transitions in coverage, providing clear and accessible explanations 
of PA requirements, and enhancing real-time and electronic PA (ePA) capabilities. Importantly, the commitments, 
which align with CMS’s broader objective to modernize PA processes and improve patient access to care, also 
include specific, time-bound targets to accelerate decision-making. 
 
Demonstrable and measurable progress has been made towards these commitments. Since June 2025, Cigna has 
reduced the overall volume of medical PAs by approximately 15%, and we are working with other leading health 
plans to advance greater standardization in ePA submission requirements for commonly reviewed medical 
services. We expect this standardization to apply to more than 70% of PA volume by the end of 2026. These 
results demonstrate that meaningful improvement is achievable through aligned incentives, standardized data 
exchange, and scalable automation – without unnecessary regulatory complexity.  
 
In parallel, Cigna has played a leading and active role in the CMS Health Technology Ecosystem (HTE), which 
seeks to advance a more connected, API-enabled infrastructure that supports secure, real-time data exchange 
between payers, providers, and technology partners. Through our engagement as co-lead of the Payer Workgroup, 
Cigna has helped develop approaches to FHIR-based PA, provider directory interoperability, and workflow-
integrated data exchange, with the goal of reducing friction in provider-payer interactions and improving the 
overall care experience. Participation in the HTE reflects Cigna’s broader strategy to position interoperability as a 
core enabler of administrative simplification and clinical efficiency. 
 
This experience underscores faster, more reliable PA decisions require coordinated policy, technology, and 
workflow transformation. CMS should build on existing industry progress, reinforce standards-based 
interoperability, and avoid requirements that would disrupt implementation already underway.  
 
b. Key Recommendations 
Cigna supports CMS’s overarching objectives in the Proposed Rule to modernize PA processes, expand electronic 
data exchange, improve transparency, and reduce administrative burden across the healthcare system. These goals 
align closely with our enterprise focus on reducing provider abrasion, improving patient experience, and enabling 
more efficient, evidence-based care delivery through enhanced interoperability. 
 
At the same time, several aspects of the Proposed Rule risk increasing administrative burden and fragmenting 
clinical workflows if implemented without additional flexibility and clarity. These risks are most pronounced 
where policy design does not fully reflect how PA is operationalized across benefit structures, clinical use cases, 
and multi-party workflows. As CMS considers the intersection of medical and pharmacy benefit workflows, it is 
critical to recognize the role of integrated health services organizations, including pharmacy benefit managers 
(PBMs), in coordinating benefits, enabling real-time clinical decision support, and reducing fragmentation across 
the care continuum.  
 
Interoperability and PA policy should prioritize integrated, end-to-end workflows that reflect real-world 
care delivery across medical and pharmacy benefits, rather than rigid structures that increase 
fragmentation. To that end, we remain concerned that payers are required to continue developing new 
  
 
 
 
3 
 
functionality to support ePA using FHIR while similar requirements do not exist for providers.1 Effective ePA 
requires meaningful participation from both payers and providers; however, while current policies require payers 
to implement ePA capabilities, providers are not required to use these channels and may continue to rely on 
manual processes such as fax and phone, limiting adoption and perpetuating fragmentation across submission 
pathways.  
 
Payer investments in API-based workflows cannot fully deliver intended efficiencies unless providers also 
implement or integrate ePA solutions within their clinical systems. To address this imbalance, CMS should 
move beyond attestation-based measures toward performance-based requirements and incorporate ePA utilization 
into quality programs or Conditions of Participation. This will accelerate provider adoption of ePA APIs and 
enable more consistent, scalable end-to-end PA workflows. 
 
With that context in mind, Cigna’s principal recommendations to CMS are as follows: 
• 
Establish a realistic implementation timeline of at least 24 months following publication of the final 
rule and associated guidance. 
• 
Ensure ePA standards are applied reasonably, allowing for: (1) flexibility to provide provider-friendly 
PA interfaces; (2) exceptions to the proposed dual-standards regulatory framework for drug regimen or 
protocol-based PA requests spanning both medical benefit drugs and pharmacy benefit drugs; (3) 
recognition that timelines for the PA process apply to complete requests; and (4) “specific reasons” for 
denials to reflect clinical nuance and varied state requirements.  
• 
Streamline reporting requirements to reduce duplication and ensure consistent, meaningful metrics 
across federal and state programs. 
• 
Limit API endpoint reporting to essential technical metadata and include safeguards for security and 
proprietary system information. 
 
II. Implementation Timelines 
The proposed implementation timelines are not operationally feasible given the complexity of the required system 
changes. Drug PA API implementation – particularly for medical benefit drugs – will require substantial multi-
system build, integration, and testing. Insufficient time for implementation could lead to rushed deployments, 
system instability, and disruption to patients and providers. These timelines are especially challenging in light of 
existing interoperability compliance obligations already underway. 
To ensure successful implementation, we urge CMS and the Office of the National Coordinator (ONC) to 
establish a timeline of at least 24 months following publication of the final rule and associated guidance. 
CMS should also adopt a phased implementation approach that prioritize mature capabilities and allow for 
iterative adoption. 
 
III. Electronic Prior Authorization (ePA) for Drugs (Section II.B.) 
Cigna supports timely access to appropriate, evidence-based interventions and views ePA as essential to reducing 
burden and improving turnaround times. 
 
CMS proposes a dual-standards approach for ePA for drugs, requiring the use of FHIR-based APIs for drugs 
covered under the medical benefit and National Council for Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards for 
drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit. Cigna strongly supports this proposed dual-standards approach for 
 
1 MIPS does not currently require providers to adopt ePA in a mandatory, operational sense. MIPS functions as an incentive and reporting mechanism – not a 
true adoption requirement. MIPS uses attestation-based measures to encourage use of ePA APIs. This means providers may need to report or attest that they 
have engaged with ePA functionality in some limited way, but they are not required to routinely use ePA for all PA requests and there is no broad mandate 
requiring full adoption or workflow integration.  
  
 
 
 
4 
 
ePA of drugs. This approach reflects existing technical ecosystems and is the most practical framework for ePA of 
drugs. 
 
PBMs play a critical role in enabling intelligent routing, given their visibility into formulary design, utilization 
management protocols, and pharmacy benefit adjudication systems. In some circumstances, however, providers 
may not have visibility into how a specific drug is classified into or across benefit structures. This challenge may 
be compounded by variation across payers, clients, delegated arrangements, and regulatory markets. Absent 
appropriate flexibility, providers may be required to determine the correct submission pathway without sufficient 
information, leading to misrouted requests, duplicative submissions, and avoidable delays in care. 
 
To address this issue, CMS should permit payers, PBMs and electronic health record (EHR) vendors the 
flexibility to enable provider-friendly interfaces. Specifically, CMS should explicitly allow providers to submit a 
PA request through a single entry point, with the request routed internally to the appropriate adjudication pathway. 
Whether through enforcement discretion or a safe harbor, this flexibility would reduce provider confusion, limit 
duplicate submissions, and improve consistency.  
 
In addition, notwithstanding Cigna’s overall support for the proposed dual-standards approach, we recommend 
CMS provide room for an exception where payers – in specific, limited circumstances – would like to issue PAs 
for regimens or protocols involving both medical and pharmacy benefit drugs to prevent increased provider 
burden and workflow fragmentation.  
 
From a clinical perspective, these issues may be significant for patients who need, and providers who prescribe, 
complex or specialty therapies, particularly for medical oncology where treatment decisions are best made at the 
episode-of-care or regimen level. For example, in acute myeloid leukemia maintenance therapy, a treatment 
regimen may include both injectable agents (e.g., decitabine or azacitidine) typically processed under the medical 
benefit and oral targeted therapies (e.g., midostaurin, gilteritinib, or quizartinib) processed under the pharmacy 
benefit. While each drug may appear appropriate when reviewed individually, the clinical appropriateness of the 
regimen depends on how these therapies are combined and sequenced. For these therapies, if PA requests are split 
between medical and pharmacy workflows, the reviewing entity may only see part of the regimen, creating risk 
that each component is approved independently even when the combination would not be supported by clinical 
evidence. 
 
Similarly, in endometrial cancer treatment for MSI-H tumors, an oral agent such as lenvatinib may be approved as 
a monotherapy under the pharmacy benefit, while pembrolizumab is reviewed separately under the medical 
benefit. However, clinical guidelines may not support the use of these therapies in combination for certain tumor 
profiles. When PA is conducted separately for each drug, the reviewing entities may lack visibility as to full 
treatment intent, resulting in approvals that do not align with evidence-based standards and potentially requiring 
rework or therapy modification after the fact. 
 
A broader class of examples can be observed with tumor-agnostic therapies and immunotherapies, where oral 
drugs (e.g., larotrectinib, dabrafenib/trametinib) are approved for specific molecular markers and may be 
requested alongside biologic agents such as pembrolizumab. When requests are split across different benefit 
pathways, each drug may meet coverage criteria in isolation, but the combination may not be clinically indicated. 
This creates risk of inconsistent decision-making and undermines the ability to perform a holistic clinical review, 
increasing the risk of inappropriate treatment. 
 
In these specific cases, in addition to clinical risks, requiring separate PA submissions for different components of 
a regimen can create substantial administrative inefficiencies. If bright lines are drawn to separate PA processes 
and standards for the medical and pharmacy benefits, many providers would need to enter the same clinical 
  
 
 
 
5 
 
documentation multiple times across different systems, increasing administrative burden and the likelihood of 
inconsistencies. If one component of a regimen is delayed or denied while another is approved, the provider may 
need to file for an exception or peer-to-peer review, appeal, and even potentially redesign treatment plans, further 
delaying care. 
 
These fragmented workflows can also have direct implications for the patient experience. For example, if a patient 
arrives at a pharmacy to fill a prescription that is part of a broader regimen, but the associated PA is still pending 
or routed incorrectly, treatment may be delayed, requiring additional provider outreach and potentially additional 
patient visits.  
 
Together, these examples illustrate that for certain complex drug therapy regimens (particularly in medical 
oncology), PA is most effectively evaluated at the regimen or protocol level. To require bifurcated workflows 
without exception may risk incomplete clinical evaluation, duplicative administrative work, and delays in 
treatment initiation – outcomes that would run counter to CMS’s goal of reducing administrative burden and 
improving efficiency. Enabling integrated, regimen-based PA workflows for certain use cases would allow for 
more accurate clinical review, improved operational efficiency, less administrative burden for providers, and 
better patient experience and outcomes. 
 
To address these concerns, Cigna recommends CMS explicitly enable appropriate exceptions to the dual-
standards approach to permit integrated, regimen, or protocol-based submission models. For such 
exceptions, CMS should permit payers to allow a single PA request to encompass all drugs (across medical 
and pharmacy benefits) within a treatment regimen, with flexibility on the standard to be used.  
 
IV. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes (Section II.C.3.) 
Cigna supports CMS’s objective to improve timeliness in PA decision-making. However, achieving this goal 
requires policies that reflect the realities of how PA requests are submitted and processed. 
 
In many instances, initial requests are submitted without sufficient clinical documentation to support a 
determination. When additional information is required, payers must request and wait for that information before 
proceeding with review. Without mechanisms to account for this dynamic, compressed decision timelines can 
result in increased denials based on incomplete submissions, leading to additional resubmissions, appeals, and 
administrative burden. 
 
We are concerned that shortened timeframes may inadvertently shift burden rather than reduce it. Specifically, 
providers may face increased requests for additional information, while patients may experience delays in care 
due to repeated submission cycles. Absent these guardrails, shortened timeframes may incentivize denials of 
incomplete requests rather than faster approvals of clinically appropriate care. 
 
Cigna recommends CMS adopt a standard whereby decision timeframes begin only once a request includes 
the minimum necessary clinical information to support review. CMS should also allow for clock-stops or 
tolling (pausing) of the required timeline when additional information is requested, with appropriate 
safeguards to ensure timely follow-up and prevent misuse.2 
 
 
2 As part of the previously mentioned industry PA voluntary commitments, Cigna and many other payers are seeking to standardize the required clinical 
elements that providers would need to submit for key interventions subject to PA. As this work progresses, providers should experience less variation among 
plans on what they need to submit in a PA request. Over time, providers should be more likely to submit a complete request at the outset, especially if they 
have experience. 
 
  
 
 
 
6 
 
Additionally, CMS should clarify how federal timeframe requirements interact with state-specific requirements, 
particularly for Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Programs, where notification requirements and 
timelines may differ. Clear alignment will be critical to avoiding duplicative or conflicting obligations. 
 
V. Denial Reason Requirements (Section II.C.2.) 
Cigna supports CMS’s proposal to require that payers provide specific reasons for PA denials. Clear and 
actionable denial communications are essential to enabling providers to respond efficiently and reduce delays in 
patient care. The effectiveness of this requirement depends on achieving an appropriate balance between clarity 
and the flexibility necessary to accommodate diverse regulatory and clinical requirements.  
 
In practice, payers must operate within a complex and evolving patchwork of state laws and regulations, many of 
which impose specific requirements regarding the content, format, and timing of denial notices. As a result, 
federal requirements that are overly rigid could create operational conflicts, increase administrative burden, and 
necessitate duplicative or fragmented approaches to compliance. 
 
Accordingly, Cigna supports CMS’s proposal because it establishes a clear requirement to provide denial 
reasons while preserving flexibility for plans to structure and present denial information in a manner that 
aligns with applicable state requirements, clinical considerations, and operational workflows. This approach 
will support meaningful communication with providers while enabling compliance across jurisdictions and 
promoting continued evolution as medical evidence and regulatory requirements change. CMS should also 
provide clear guidance on audit expectations to ensure consistent implementation and reduce compliance 
uncertainty. 
 
VI. Reporting and Transparency Requirements (Sections II.C.6.-II.C.7) 
Cigna supports CMS’s goal of improving transparency in PA processes. However, the Proposed Rule introduces 
new reporting requirements that may overlap with existing federal and state mandates, creating the potential for 
duplicative and resource-intensive reporting obligations. Variability in metric definitions and reporting levels may 
limit comparability and create misinterpretation, while duplicative reporting frameworks would require plans to 
maintain parallel processes without improving insight. 
 
CMS should align and streamline new reporting requirements by establishing standardized definitions, 
denominators, and reporting levels. CMS should also establish a single national framework for PA metrics that 
preempts duplicative state requirements. Absent federal standardization, the continued proliferation of 
inconsistent state reporting requirements will materially increase administrative burden without improving 
transparency or comparability. 
 
In addition, CMS should consider a phased approach to implementation or limit initial reporting requirements to a 
core set of prioritized metrics to ensure data quality and consistency during early adoption. 
 
VII. API Endpoint Reporting and Transparency (Section II.E.) 
Cigna supports CMS’s objective of improving interoperability by increasing visibility into payer API endpoints. 
However, the scope of reporting must be carefully managed to avoid unintended consequences. Overly broad 
reporting requirements could expose sensitive information related to system architecture, introduce cybersecurity 
risks, and potentially extend into areas beyond interoperability, such as network design. 
 
To mitigate these risks, we recommend CMS limit endpoint reporting requirements to essential technical 
metadata necessary to facilitate connectivity, such as base URLs, capability statements, and supported 
standards. CMS should also implement safeguards to protect proprietary information and establish clear processes 
  
 
 
 
7 
 
for updating and validating endpoint data. Importantly, CMS should clarify that endpoint reporting is intended 
solely to support interoperability rather than be used to expand transparency requirements into unrelated domains. 
 
VIII. Conclusion 
CMS should prioritize policies that measure real-world performance – such as speed, completeness, and usability 
of PA workflows – rather than prescriptive technical requirements that may not translate into improved outcomes.  
 
We appreciate CMS’s leadership in advancing interoperability and PA reform. With targeted refinements – 
particularly those that support integrated workflows, alignment of reporting requirements, and realistic 
implementation timelines – the final rule can achieve its intended goals while minimizing unintended burden. 
 
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. Please note we are attaching an appendix containing further 
comments in response to the RFIs issued by CMS and ONC.  
 
We look forward to continued collaboration and stand ready to support CMS in developing practical, scalable 
solutions that improve outcomes for patients, providers, and the healthcare system overall. 
 
 
Respectfully, 
 
 
Courtney Lawrence  
Senior Vice President  
Head of Government Affairs and Global Public Policy 
 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
8 
 
APPENDIX: 
Requests for Information (RFIs) 
 
We appreciate the inclusion of Requests for Information with the CMS-0062-P Proposed Rule and are pleased to 
share the comments below. 
 
A. Electronic Event Notifications (Section III.A.) 
 
I.  
Use and Content of Patient Event Notifications 
We appreciate CMS’s continued focus on advancing patient electronic event notifications as a foundational 
mechanism to improve care coordination and transitions of care. Our experience as a national payer operating 
across multiple lines of business highlights that variability in notification content, structure, and reliability now 
limits the scalability and practical utility of these notifications for care coordination and downstream workflows. 
 
To address these limitations, CMS should prioritize greater standardization while preserving flexibility and 
minimizing provider burden. We recommend CMS consider incorporating a defined set of high-value, structured 
data elements, such as event type and timing, high-level clinical indicators, discharge disposition, and care team 
contact information. The inclusion of these elements would materially improve the usability of notifications for 
care management and coordination activities, while maintaining a pragmatic scope. 
 
At the same time, any expansion of notification content should be grounded in the principle of minimizing 
clinician burden. CMS should prioritize the use of structured, system-generated data that can be automatically 
populated from existing workflows, rather than introducing additional manual documentation requirements. 
Consistent with this objective, we support a “notify and query” model in which notifications provide sufficient 
context to inform downstream action, while enabling authorized recipients to retrieve more detailed clinical 
information through standards-based APIs. This approach aligns with emerging FHIR-based frameworks and 
provides a scalable pathway to balance data availability with operational efficiency. 
 
As CMS considers expanding notification content, it will also be critical to ensure that data sharing remains 
aligned with applicable privacy and data governance standards. Expanded notifications should adhere to minimum 
necessary principles and be supported by robust authorization frameworks to ensure that information is shared 
only with entities that have a legitimate role in the patient’s care. In addition, improving the accuracy of provider 
and organizational directories, as well as recipient identification processes, will be essential to ensuring that 
notifications are delivered reliably and to the intended parties. 
 
II. 
Types of Providers and Entities Receiving Notifications 
We recognize the significant opportunity to expand the reach and value of patient event notifications by enabling 
broader participation across the care ecosystem, including payers, accountable care organizations, and post-acute 
providers. As a payer, we currently leverage event notifications to support care management interventions, 
facilitate post-discharge follow-up, and improve coordination across providers – activities that contribute directly 
to improved member outcomes and reduced avoidable utilization. However, the current ecosystem remains 
fragmented and heavily dependent on non-scalable, point-to-point integrations. 
 
Several persistent challenges continue to limit broader and more effective participation. These include difficulty 
consistently identifying appropriate recipients, variability in patient attribution methodologies, and inconsistencies 
in consent and authorization requirements. Absent a more structured approach, these challenges will continue to 
constrain the effectiveness of expanded notification policies. 
 
  
 
 
 
9 
 
To address these issues, CMS should prioritize the adoption of standardized attribution and subscription-based 
models that allow authorized entities to proactively receive notifications for attributed populations. This would 
shift the responsibility for identifying appropriate recipients away from individual hospitals, reducing provider 
burden while improving both the accuracy and completeness of notification delivery. Existing standards, such as 
the HL7 Da Vinci Member Attribution List Implementation Guide, provide a clear and scalable path forward. 
 
As CMS considers expanding the types of entities eligible to receive notifications, we encourage a targeted and 
risk-based approach. While inclusion of additional stakeholders, such as behavioral health providers or social 
service organizations, may enhance care coordination, such expansion must be accompanied by appropriate 
privacy safeguards and a careful assessment of operational complexity. In parallel, targeted support for post-acute 
and long-term care providers – particularly through shared infrastructure and intermediary models – will be 
critical to ensuring equitable participation across the ecosystem. 
 
III. 
Complementary Policy Approaches 
We support CMS’s use of complementary policy levers to advance adoption and effective use of patient event 
notifications, rather than relying exclusively on expanded Conditions of Participation. Existing programs, 
including the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program, offer a more flexible and scalable pathway to drive 
progress while aligning incentives with desired outcomes. 
 
In this context, CMS should prioritize policies that emphasize the effectiveness and usability of patient 
notifications, rather than simply increasing their volume. Incentive structures should reward the successful 
delivery of notifications to appropriate authorized recipients and encourage improvements in timeliness and 
reliability. This outcomes-based approach will better align stakeholder behavior with the underlying objective of 
improving care coordination. 
 
Additionally, CMS should continue to promote adoption of standards-based technical approaches, particularly 
those aligned with FHIR, to reduce variability and fragmentation across implementations. Close coordination with 
ONC will be critical to ensuring alignment between policy requirements and certification criteria, particularly 
with respect to supporting subscription-based models and scalable interoperability frameworks. 
 
We also view the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) as a valuable complementary 
pathway to scale notification exchange at a national level. By leveraging TEFCA, CMS can reduce reliance on 
point-to-point integrations, establish trust among participating entities, and expand the reach of notifications to 
authorized stakeholders across the care continuum. However, in its current form, TEFCA remains limited in its 
ability to support payer use cases at scale – including critical workflows such as ePA. To fully realize TEFCA’s 
potential for payers, ONC should require responses for the Payment and Healthcare Operations Exchange 
Purposes and ensure that any fees being charged to payers are reasonable, do not impede participation, and are not 
for access to the data itself (but could be related to optional value-added services). Absent these changes, the 
framework will provide limited value to payers and will not effectively support broader adoption of interoperable, 
FHIR-based exchange beyond the Treatment and Individual Access Services Exchange Purposes. 
 
IV. 
Technical Approaches 
While CMS’s current flexible approach to technical implementation has supported early adoption, it has also 
contributed to significant fragmentation across HL7 v2 messaging, C-CDA documents, and FHIR-based APIs. 
This variability creates inefficiencies and limits the ability to scale notification exchange in a consistent and 
interoperable manner. 
 
We recommend CMS take steps to promote convergence toward modern, standards-based approaches, particularly 
those grounded in FHIR and supported by emerging HL7 Da Vinci implementation guides. Frameworks such as 
  
 
 
 
10 
 
the Da Vinci Unsolicited Notifications Implementation Guide provide a more consistent and scalable foundation 
for event-driven data exchange, while enabling a “notify and query” architecture that enhances usability. 
 
The adoption of FHIR-based subscription models represents a particularly important opportunity to improve 
efficiency and scalability. These models allow authorized entities to define and manage notification preferences in 
a more dynamic and configurable manner, reducing the need for custom integrations and improving overall 
system performance. 
 
Given the current level of ecosystem variability, we recommend a phased implementation approach that begins 
with incentives and guidance to encourage voluntary adoption of these advanced frameworks, with a gradual 
transition toward more formal expectations as standards mature and implementation experience expands. 
Concurrently, CMS should continue to prioritize improvements in patient matching, identity resolution, and 
authorization processes, which remain foundational to accurate and secure notification delivery. 
 
V. 
Enforcement 
We support CMS’s continued use of existing survey and certification mechanisms to enforce compliance with 
patient event notification requirements, as these approaches have effectively established a baseline level of 
implementation while preserving necessary flexibility. As CMS considers enhancements to enforcement, it will be 
important to maintain this balance and avoid overly prescriptive requirements that could impede innovation or 
create unintended operational burden. 
 
Enforcement efforts should focus on process maturity and reasonable effort standards, rather than mandating 
specific technical solutions. CMS should also prioritize metrics that reflect the effectiveness of notification 
delivery, such as successful routing and reductions in undeliverable messages, as these measures more directly 
align with the intended outcomes of the policy. 
 
Finally, any strengthening of enforcement should be implemented through a phased approach that accounts for 
external dependencies, including directory accuracy, attribution models, and interoperability infrastructure, which 
are not solely within the control of individual stakeholders. CMS can also play a critical role in supporting 
compliance by providing technical assistance, clear implementation guidance, and best practices to help 
stakeholders operationalize requirements effectively. 
 
B. Increasing Healthcare Resiliency (Section III.B.) 
 
I.  
Cybersecurity 
We appreciate CMS’s focus on strengthening cybersecurity and resiliency across the healthcare ecosystem. Cyber 
threats – particularly ransomware – have increasingly demonstrated that cybersecurity is integral not only to 
protecting health information, but also to maintaining continuity of care, operational stability, and patient safety. 
National analyses have shown that cyber disruptions can meaningfully degrade the health system’s ability to 
deliver care, particularly when combined with broader capacity and workforce pressures.  
 
Existing statutes and requirements within CMS’s purview have appropriately elevated cybersecurity as a core 
operational priority. However, the broader regulatory landscape remains fragmented across multiple agencies, 
resulting in overlapping expectations that can dilute focus on the most impactful risk reduction activities. Prior 
federal work has emphasized that inconsistent or duplicative requirements across agencies can impose significant 
burden without materially improving security outcomes, underscoring the importance of alignment and 
harmonization.  
 
  
 
 
 
11 
 
Looking forward, CMS can further strengthen the system by prioritizing outcome-oriented resilience capabilities 
rather than prescriptive, technology-specific requirements. We believe the most effective approach is to focus on 
whether organizations can (1) maintain or rapidly restore critical operations, (2) respond effectively to incidents, 
and (3) prevent high-impact events such as ransomware-related disruptions. 
 
Across the healthcare sector, several systemic challenges continue to limit cybersecurity maturity. These include 
the growing sophistication and frequency of cyberattacks; complex interdependencies across providers, payers, 
clearinghouses, and vendors; and resource constraints, particularly for small and rural providers. Cyberattacks can 
have significant downstream operational impacts. For example, prolonged system outages can disrupt claims 
processing and revenue flows, contributing to financial distress and, in some cases, facility closures. At the same 
time, rising cyber risk has increased insurance premiums and reduced availability of insurance coverage, further 
constraining organizations’ ability to absorb and recover from cyber events.  
 
We support CMS advancing a framework that promotes high-impact resilience capabilities, including: 
• 
Robust incident response and business continuity planning, with regular testing; 
• 
Reliable data recovery and restoration processes; 
• 
Strong identity and access controls; and 
• 
Continuous workforce training tailored to real-world threats such as phishing and social engineering. 
 
In addition, CMS should recognize that cybersecurity is an ecosystem challenge. Dependencies on intermediaries 
– particularly clearinghouses and third-party technology vendors – create systemic risk that can amplify the 
impact of a disruption. Improving resilience therefore requires not only individual organizational preparedness but 
also greater coordination and contingency planning across interconnected entities. 
 
Finally, we strongly encourage CMS to ensure that any expanded expectations are paired with practical 
implementation support, particularly for small, rural, and resource-constrained providers. Without such support, 
increased requirements risk exacerbating disparities in cybersecurity maturity and could unintentionally contribute 
to financial strain or consolidation. 
 
II.  
Standards and Technologies 
We support CMS’s focus on the relationship between interoperability and cybersecurity and agree that standards 
and technologies should be evaluated with the objective of enhancing resilience while minimizing fragmentation 
and complexity. Expanded interoperability and API-driven data exchange create meaningful opportunities to 
modernize infrastructure and improve real-time exchange across stakeholders, but they also inherently increase 
cybersecurity risk and amplify existing challenges related to data integrity and system complexity. 
 
The current environment reflects a significant degree of variability in how interoperability standards are 
implemented and secured. While prior CMS interoperability efforts have advanced data exchange, they have also 
contributed to an expansion in the number of endpoints, interfaces, and third-party connections that must be 
secured. This expanded API-based connectivity increases exposure to cybersecurity threats, including 
unauthorized access and data misappropriation. In addition, the lack of a unified data standard across medical and 
pharmacy ecosystems – including the continued divide between FHIR and NCPDP – creates ongoing risks to data 
accuracy and integrity and can introduce friction in end-to-end workflows. 
 
To address these challenges, we recommend CMS align requirements with recognized cybersecurity frameworks, 
such as National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), to promote consistency and strengthen baseline 
security practices across the industry. CMS should also promote greater standardization across data formats and 
exchange approaches so that interoperability advances do not further entrench fragmented implementation 
  
 
 
 
12 
 
models. At the same time, CMS can help reduce implementation burden by providing clear guidance and, where 
appropriate, support mechanisms that enable more consistent and equitable adoption across stakeholders. 
 
In this context, coordination across federal agencies is essential. Interoperability and cybersecurity requirements 
should be aligned so that organizations are not subject to duplicative or conflicting expectations. This is 
particularly important given the significant cost and operational burden associated with building and maintaining 
complex, multi-system API environments. 
 
We also see significant potential for national frameworks such as TEFCA to support resiliency goals. TEFCA is 
designed to establish a common governance, policy, and technical foundation for data exchange, reduce reliance 
on fragmented point-to-point connections, and strengthen privacy and security requirements across participating 
networks. By providing a more unified and scalable architecture, TEFCA can improve the reliability and 
continuity of data exchange, particularly during disruptions affecting individual organizations or networks.  
 
More broadly, interoperability policies should be designed to enhance security by design, ensuring expansion of 
data exchange capabilities does not inadvertently increase systemic risk. This includes limiting unnecessary 
proliferation of endpoints, promoting consistent security practices, and ensuring that data exchange is both trusted 
and resilient. 
 
III.  
Point-to-Point Connections 
We recognize that point-to-point connections have historically enabled flexible and tailored data exchange across 
healthcare stakeholders. However, reliance on large numbers of bespoke connections introduces significant 
challenges for both security and resiliency. As the number of direct integrations grows, organizations must secure 
and maintain an increasingly complex network of connections. This can create operational fragility, particularly 
when individual connections or intermediary entities are disrupted. National interoperability efforts, including 
TEFCA, have sought to reduce reliance on one-off connections by providing a more scalable, network-based 
model for exchange.  
 
Clearinghouses play a critical role in facilitating administrative transactions and supporting connectivity across 
providers and payers. At the same time, they can represent concentrated points of dependency, meaning that 
disruptions at the clearinghouse level can have cascading impacts across the system. Ensuring resiliency therefore 
requires improved contingency planning, redundancy, and transition capabilities. 
 
We recommend CMS consider policies and guidance that: 
• 
Enable greater portability and standardization across clearinghouses; 
• 
Support rapid transition and failover capabilities during disruptions; and 
• 
Reduce the complexity and cost associated with switching or onboarding alternative intermediaries when 
necessary. 
 
Ultimately, a more resilient system will rely less on fragile, individualized connections and more on standardized, 
secure, and scalable exchange frameworks. Supporting this transition will be critical to improving both 
operational continuity and cybersecurity posture across the healthcare ecosystem. 
 
C. Improving Implementation of Payer Application Programming Interface Technology (Section 
III.C.) 
 
I. 
Roadmap for Consistent Implementation of Payer API Technology 
We appreciate CMS’s focus on advancing a more consistent and scalable approach to payer API implementation. 
As API capabilities continue to expand across patient access, PA, provider data exchange, and payer-to-payer use 
  
 
 
 
13 
 
cases, ensuring consistent implementation and reliable performance is essential to delivering on the goals of 
interoperability – namely, reducing provider burden, improving patient experience, and enabling real-time, 
actionable data exchange. 
 
We believe the most significant challenges associated with payer API implementation are not rooted in the 
availability of technical standards, but rather in the variation in how those standards are implemented, interpreted, 
and operationalized in production environments. Despite the maturation of FHIR-based implementation guides 
(IGs), variability persists across data mapping, endpoint configurations, authentication workflows, and 
performance expectations. This variability creates friction for providers, payers, health IT developers, and 
downstream users, ultimately limiting the usability and scalability of these APIs. 
 
To address these issues, CMS should focus on establishing a clear, phased roadmap for API implementation 
maturity, grounded in these foundational principles: 
• 
Consistency of implementation across payers and health IT developers; 
• 
Real-world usability and performance (beyond theoretical conformance); 
• 
Minimization of unnecessary burden on both payers and health IT developers. 
 
Oversight and Testing Approach 
We support the development of structured but flexible oversight mechanisms that promote consistent API 
performance without introducing excessive compliance burden. We believe the most impactful oversight models 
will focus on validating that APIs: accurately implement standardized data elements and workflows; perform 
reliably under real-world conditions (including response times and availability); and support seamless integration 
with provider and third-party systems. 
 
Rather than imposing highly prescriptive or duplicative testing requirements, CMS should adopt a risk-based, 
targeted testing approach, prioritizing areas where variability has the greatest impact on the ecosystem. These 
include: 
• 
Authentication and authorization workflows (e.g., OAuth2 implementation consistency); 
• 
Data completeness and accuracy, particularly for clinical and administrative data used in care 
coordination and PA; 
• 
End-to-end workflow functionality, such as request/response cycles for PA or data access use cases. 
 
We believe testing should evolve beyond basic conformance validation and incorporate functional and 
interoperability testing across systems, ensuring that APIs are not only technically compliant but also 
interoperable in practice. Testing should simulate real-world multi-party interactions (e.g., payer–provider–health 
IT developer scenarios), where many current issues arise. 
 
Testing Frameworks, Platforms, and Tools 
We support CMS encouraging the use of standardized, industry-aligned testing frameworks to drive consistency 
while minimizing duplication. Testing platforms should be transparent, open, and widely accessible to both payers 
and vendors; support modular testing, allowing organizations to validate specific components independently; 
enable automated and repeatable testing, reducing operational burden; and reflect real-world workflows and use 
cases, rather than purely synthetic test scenarios. 
 
The identification and evaluation of testing tools should focus on the ability to: 
• 
Align with recognized IGs; 
• 
Support both conformance and functional testing; 
• 
Scale across multiple use cases and evolving standards; 
  
 
 
 
14 
 
• 
Integrate into existing development and deployment pipelines. 
 
Importantly, CMS should avoid mandating a single tool and instead support a flexible ecosystem of validated 
tools, with clear criteria for inclusion. This approach will encourage innovation while maintaining a baseline level 
of trust and consistency. 
 
Real-World Interoperability Testing 
We strongly support CMS exploring requirements for interoperability testing across multiple systems, particularly 
as API ecosystems mature. Conformance testing alone does not ensure that systems can effectively exchange data 
in production environments, where differences in interpretation, configuration, and system behavior can create 
barriers. 
 
A phased approach to interoperability testing could include initial voluntary pilots or demonstration programs; 
development of shared testing scenarios and datasets; and gradual incorporation into program expectations as 
standards stabilize. This approach will allow CMS to advance interoperability in a measured and practical manner, 
ensuring that testing requirements are aligned with industry readiness. 
 
II. 
Certification of Payer API Technology 
We are concerned about the certification of payer API technology at this time, whether as a mandatory 
requirement or as a voluntary program that CMS would rely upon to demonstrate compliance. We support 
consistent implementation of payer APIs and robust testing, but believe certification would be overly burdensome, 
misaligned with the statutory design of the 21st Century Cures Act (Cures Act), and likely to create unintended 
regulatory consequences that would ultimately slow interoperability progress rather than accelerate it.  
 
Unlike EHR certification – which is built around a comparatively bounded set of clinical workflows and a discrete 
class of “certified health IT” – payer API implementation spans a highly heterogeneous technology environment. 
Payers typically operate a multi-vendor ecosystem of claims platforms, care management systems, PBM systems, 
member portals, delegated vendor arrangements, and line-of-business-specific infrastructure. Requiring 
certification of “payer API technology” would force payers to align diverse architectures to a single certification 
model, driving substantial cost and administrative complexity that is unlikely to translate into practical 
improvements in interoperability.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Courtney Lawrence, Senior Vice President, Head of Government Affairs and Global Public Policy, The Cigna Group.
- **Stakeholder type:** Payer / PBM / integrated health services organization.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Cigna describes national commercial medical coverage, Evernorth pharmacy and specialty pharmacy services, PBM capabilities, participation in the CMS Health Technology Ecosystem, and co-leadership of the Payer Workgroup.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Cigna supports CMS's goals to modernize prior authorization, expand electronic data exchange, improve transparency, and reduce administrative burden, but urges CMS to add flexibility and a longer implementation runway. The comment's central requests are a minimum 24-month implementation period after final guidance, provider adoption requirements for ePA, flexible routing across medical/pharmacy benefit boundaries, streamlined reporting, and narrowly scoped API endpoint reporting with cybersecurity protections.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; GENERAL/RFIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P generally; no detailed CFR citations beyond references to Sections II.B, II.C.2, II.C.3, II.C.6-II.C.7, II.E, and RFI sections.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR, Da Vinci prior authorization approaches, NCPDP, HL7 Da Vinci Member Attribution List IG, Da Vinci Unsolicited Notifications IG, TEFCA, NIST, API endpoint metadata, OAuth-like authorization concepts, EHR/ePA integration.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Implementation timeline**
- **Provision ID:** IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY / FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Drug PA API implementation requires multi-system build, integration, testing, and coordination with other interoperability obligations. A rushed timeline could create instability and disruption for patients and providers.
- **Specific request:** Establish at least 24 months after publication of the final rule and associated guidance, and use phased implementation that prioritizes mature capabilities.

**Topic 2: Dual standards and integrated benefit workflows**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** Cigna supports FHIR for medical benefit drugs and NCPDP for pharmacy benefit drugs, but says providers often cannot determine benefit classification and complex regimens may span both benefits.
- **Specific request:** Allow a provider-friendly single entry point with internal routing, and create exceptions for integrated regimen- or protocol-based PA requests that span medical and pharmacy benefit drugs.

**Topic 3: Provider adoption of ePA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Payer API investments will not deliver efficiency if providers are not required to use or integrate ePA and continue fax/phone/portal workflows.
- **Specific request:** Move beyond attestation-based measures and incorporate ePA utilization into quality programs or Conditions of Participation.

**Topic 4: Drug PA decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify / clarify.
- **Rationale:** Incomplete submissions can require additional clinical information; compressed clocks may increase denials and resubmissions if the timeline runs before a complete request is available.
- **Specific request:** Start decision clocks only when minimum necessary clinical information is received; allow clock-stops/tolling while awaiting additional information; clarify interaction with state-specific Medicaid and CHIP timelines.

**Topic 5: Denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with flexibility.
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons are important, but payers must comply with varied state notice requirements and clinical nuance.
- **Specific request:** Preserve flexibility in format and presentation and provide audit guidance.

**Topic 6: Reporting and endpoint transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Overlapping federal and state metrics can be duplicative; overly broad endpoint reporting may expose system architecture or proprietary information.
- **Specific request:** Standardize metrics and denominators, consider phased reporting, preempt duplicative state reporting where appropriate, limit endpoint reporting to base URLs, capability statements, and supported standards, and protect sensitive information.

**Topic 7: RFIs on event notifications, resiliency, payer APIs, step therapy, lab tests, and DMEPOS**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFIs; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Mixed / modify.
- **Rationale:** Cigna supports standardization, FHIR-aligned notify-and-query models, TEFCA improvements, NIST-aligned cybersecurity, testing over certification for payer APIs, and pragmatic automation of step therapy, labs, and DMEPOS.
- **Specific request:** Use phased guidance, avoid payer API certification, enable standards-based testing, support lab coding solutions, and balance DMEPOS access with program integrity.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S15/S21/S28:** Supports dual medical/pharmacy standards but requests provider-friendly routing and exceptions for integrated regimen-level PA; requests at least 24 months after final guidance.
- **S16/S17:** Supports specific denial reasons but requests flexibility for clinical nuance and state-law variation.
- **S20/S43:** Requests decision timeframes begin only once a complete request is received and allow tolling when more information is needed.
- **S23/S24/S26/S27/S33:** Supports endpoint visibility but recommends limiting reporting to essential technical metadata and safeguarding proprietary/cybersecurity-sensitive information.
- **S29/S30/S34/S35:** Requests streamlined metrics, standardized definitions, and phased reporting to reduce duplication and improve comparability.
- **S44-S56:** Addresses HIPAA implications indirectly through concern about FHIR requirements, workflow transformation, and the need for practical timelines and flexibility.
- **S60-S65:** Supports updated standards with phased adoption, guidance, and testing; warns against fragmented or premature mandates.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on event notifications, resiliency, payer API implementation, certification, step therapy, labs, and DMEPOS with recommendations for standardized, phased, and outcomes-based approaches.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Provide at least 24 months after final rule and guidance before compliance.
2. Permit a single provider entry point for drug PA with payer/PBM/EHR routing to the correct benefit pathway.
3. Create exceptions allowing integrated regimen/protocol PA across medical and pharmacy benefits.
4. Require stronger provider-side ePA adoption through performance-based requirements or quality programs.
5. Begin PA decision clocks only after complete clinical information is submitted and allow tolling.
6. Preserve flexibility in denial-reason formats and issue clear audit guidance.
7. Streamline and standardize reporting metrics, reducing duplicative state and federal obligations.
8. Limit endpoint reporting to essential metadata and protect cybersecurity/proprietary information.
9. Use conformance/interoperability testing rather than payer API certification.
10. Support FHIR-aligned event notification, TEFCA payer use cases, lab coding improvements, and DMEPOS program integrity.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Implementation timeline, provider non-adoption of ePA, rigid dual-standard boundaries, fragmented reporting, endpoint security, certification burden.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Misrouted drug PA requests, duplicate submissions, delayed therapy, incomplete clinical review, increased administrative burden, rushed deployments, cybersecurity exposure.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Multi-system integration, EHR adoption, provider workflow integration, state-law variation, PBM/payer/vendor coordination, standards variability, lab coding gaps.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Cigna reports reducing overall medical PA volume by about 15% since June 2025 and expects standardization for more than 70% of PA volume by the end of 2026; it cites CMS fraud figures for DMEPOS in the RFI appendix.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Federal cybersecurity/resiliency analyses and CMS healthcare fraud takedown are referenced; details are mostly summarized rather than deeply analyzed.
- **Examples provided:** Oncology regimens involving injectable and oral therapies across benefit structures; acute myeloid leukemia, endometrial cancer, tumor-agnostic therapies, lab test coding, and DMEPOS fraud examples.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Payers, PBMs, EHR vendors, providers, Medicaid/CHIP programs, QHPs, patients, pharmacies, labs, DME suppliers, clearinghouses, app/API developers.
- **Economic implications:** Significant implementation and reporting costs; potential savings from automation and reduced duplicate submissions; potential increased costs from certification or fragmented workflows.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if phased, tested, and flexible; risky if mandates are compressed or rigid.
- **Patient care impact:** Cigna argues integrated and automated workflows can reduce delays, while rigid benefit-split processes can delay specialty and oncology treatment.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed / concerned supportive.
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, collaborative.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Interoperability and PA policy should prioritize integrated, end-to-end workflows that reflect real-world care delivery across medical and pharmacy benefits" - Context: Core recommendation on avoiding fragmented dual-standard workflows.
2. "Establish a realistic implementation timeline of at least 24 months following publication of the final rule and associated guidance." - Context: Key recommendation on compliance timing.
3. "CMS should explicitly enable appropriate exceptions to the dual-standards approach to permit integrated, regimen, or protocol-based submission models." - Context: Recommendation for complex therapies spanning benefits.
4. "Limit endpoint reporting requirements to essential technical metadata necessary to facilitate connectivity" - Context: API endpoint reporting and security recommendation.
